Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (StratusHealth - Head of Platform), Evan Cole (ML Infra), Rina Gupta (SRE)

Summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Quick technical deep dive on scheduler knobs for continuous batching and handling short bursts. Discussed max_num_seqs, token limits, backpressure, kv-cache eviction, and tradeoffs of quantization on memory vs perf. Agreed on benchmark sweep and to share configs and security docs.

Topics: [continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token_limit, kv cache, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem memory]

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to get into the scheduler knobs and some practical numbers around burst handling for StratusHealth, especially given your bursty traffic pattern that Priya mentioned.
[00:18] Priya Nair: yeah hi, thanks. we're seeing kinda spiky traffic from clinical triage at 9am and 3pm, bursts that are a couple thousand requests over 2-3 minutes, and we care about p99 latency under 300ms for the sync path.
[00:35] Luca Ortiz: okay great context, quick intro — i'm Luca on the SE side. we'll go over continuous batching behavior, the max_num_seqs parameter, token limits, and then KV cache eviction and quantization considerations. feel free to interrupt.
[00:52] Evan Cole: quick q, is continuous batching the default in hosted runtime, or something we enable per-model?
[00:58] Maya Chen: it's on by default for most workloads on Redwood hosted, but on Dedicated/Private you can tune the scheduler knobs — the defaults are conservative, we expose max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, and an idle_ms threshold.
[01:13] Rina Gupta: also we'll be on-prem for the critical path, so memory and locality matter — we need to know how kv cache and quantization will affect host memory.
[01:23] Luca Ortiz: absolutely. quick mental model: continuous batching tries to fill in-sequence slots across concurrent requests while respecting per-request max_sequence length and overall token limits. max_num_seqs basically caps how many concurrent sequences the scheduler will pack into a single compute wave.
[01:40] Priya Nair: so if we set max_num_seqs too high, do we hurt p99 because slow requests hold up the batch?
[01:46] Luca Ortiz: yep that's the tradeoff. higher max_num_seqs increases throughput and GPU utilization but can increase tail latency if you have stragglers. We recommend pairing it with a per-request token_limit and a per-batch token cap so a single long request can't blow up the wave.
[02:05] Maya Chen: and remember playback/backpressure — the scheduler emits backpressure signals to the ingress when queues exceed X, that's configurable.
[02:12] Evan Cole: what's the X by default?
[02:14] Luca Ortiz: default queue high-water is 10k tokens equivalent, but on Dedicated you can lower to 2k for tight latency SLOs. that's measured in token-equivalents using the median tokenization.
[02:28] Priya Nair: can you talk about kv cache eviction? we use cached prefix hits a lot for session-based context.
[02:34] Luca Ortiz: good one. KV cache is reference-counted per-seq and we keep a live cache until memory pressure triggers eviction. eviction policy is LRU-ish but we also do size-based trimming per-GPU. When you have many short sessions, it improves perf because cache hits bypass recomputation, but if too many unique contexts accumulate you'll see increased memory and eviction churn which can create micro-pauses.
[02:56] Rina Gupta: micro-pauses would kill our p99, so do you offer pinning of a small hot-set?
[03:02] Luca Ortiz: yes, on Dedicated/Private you can pin a hot-kv-set per model and reserve memory for it — that's a config under the runtime memory policy.
[03:12] Priya Nair: what's the overhead of pinning?
[03:15] Luca Ortiz: depends on sequence length and number of keys, but for 12k tokens across sessions we typically reserve ~2–4 GB of GPU memory per pinned shard on A100-class. numbers vary with quantization.
[03:28] Evan Cole: speaking of quantization — we're exploring 4-bit quantization for cost—what are the perf trade-offs?
[03:33] Luca Ortiz: 4-bit reduces model memory footprint significantly and increases effective batch size before hitting memory limits, but it can slightly change probabilities leading to small quality delta. There are also kernel-level perf differences: int4 matmul paths are good for throughput but may have slightly different latency characteristics. We usually recommend 8-bit-LLM for latency-sensitive options and 4-bit for heavy throughput where you can accept minimal quality variance.
[03:57] Priya Nair: any gotchas with kv cache + quantization?
[04:00] Luca Ortiz: yes — when quantizing weights but keeping KV cache in fp16, you get best of both worlds; however some quant pipelines also quantize activations which complicate cache format conversions and can add CPU/GPU copy overhead.
[04:14] Maya Chen: to add — for Private deployments we give you knobs to choose cache format. default is fp16 cache for accuracy and lower conversion cost.
[04:22] Evan Cole: back to scheduler — can you explain the idle_ms threshold?
[04:26] Luca Ortiz: idle_ms is how long the scheduler will wait for additional sequences before dispatching an under-filled wave. Lower idle_ms reduces tail but can reduce utilization. Typical tuning: set max_num_seqs moderately high (64) with idle_ms low (6-12ms) for low p99 but medium overall throughput; or set idle_ms higher (20-40ms) with max_num_seqs high (128) for batchy workloads.
[04:50] Priya Nair: do you have a recommended starting config for our burst size (~2k requests over 3 minutes)?
[04:55] Luca Ortiz: start with max_num_seqs=64, token_limit=512, idle_ms=10, and a batch_token_cap of 8192. That gives headroom for bursts but keeps single long requests from monopolizing the wave. We'll test those numbers.
[05:10] Rina Gupta: how do you instrument to see real-time that a request was delayed because of batching?
[05:15] Maya Chen: Redwood console emits per-request trace with enqueue_time, dispatch_time, and device_compute_start. You can correlate enqueue->dispatch to see scheduler wait. Also we have queue length metrics by token-equivalent.
[05:28] Evan Cole: in an on-prem setup with VPC peering we need to ensure that RPC serialization for kv cache doesn't create network spikes — any advice?
[05:36] Luca Ortiz: for on-prem we recommend colocating cache shards with the serving worker to avoid cross-host KV fetches; if you must remote fetch, use async prefetch and a bounded fetch concurrency. Also enable compression on the cache wire protocol.
[05:50] Priya Nair: will the SE run a test that simulates our 2-3 minute bursts, or do we need to provide traces?
[05:56] Luca Ortiz: we'll do both — Luca will run controlled sweeps and if you provide a sample trace we can replay to replicate burstiness exactly.
[06:04] Maya Chen: quick note — for SOC2/procurement we also need to share our VPC/on-prem checklist and SOC reports, i'll action that.
[06:11] Priya Nair: thanks. also curious — how does auto-fallback work if a Dedicated node is overloaded?
[06:16] Luca Ortiz: smart routing can fallback to a lower-cost variant or to hosted pool; we can do model-variant fallbacks with cost/latency policies. In your case we might fallback to a smaller-quant model to keep latency. There is also circuit-breaker behavior if queue depth exceeds threshold.
[06:32] Evan Cole: what about max_tokens_per_batch — you mentioned batch_token_cap — how is that enforced?
[06:37] Luca Ortiz: enforced as a hard cap — scheduler sums token_lengths of sequences in the wave and won't exceed the cap. If incoming request would overflow, it either waits for next wave or, if backpressure is configured, we reject/queue based on priority.
[06:51] Rina Gupta: priority? can we mark clinical triage as higher priority?
[06:54] Maya Chen: yes, we support token/route-level priorities — you can reserve a portion of batch_token_cap for high-priority traffic.
[07:01] Priya Nair: ok. can you run through a quick example with numbers?
[07:04] Luca Ortiz: sure: assume GPU can handle 100k tokens per wave. If batch_token_cap=10000 and max_num_seqs=64 and token_limit=512, then worst case 64*512=32768 but batch_token_cap prevents that; you'll get waves shaped more evenly. If a single request is 2k tokens it will be truncated to token_limit or forced into a single smaller wave depending on your truncation policy.
[07:30] Evan Cole: truncation policy — do you allow partial streaming for long requests so they don't block?
[07:34] Luca Ortiz: streaming helps. We have per-request stream-first dispatch where model emits partial tokens as soon as available. But remember streaming still participates in the scheduler packing: you can prioritize streaming outputs.
[07:46] Priya Nair: any perf numbers from your internal tests for p99 vs qps with these knobs?
[07:50] Luca Ortiz: high level — with max_num_seqs=64 and idle_ms=10 we saw 2–2.5x throughput vs conservative defaults, p99 increased by ~20-30ms in mixed workloads. With pinning hot-kv and 8-bit quant you can often double throughput with <10% p99 shift. we'll share exact CSVs from the sweep.
[08:12] Maya Chen: (interruption) note that all numbers vary by model — gpt-like transformer with 2048 context behaves differently than a 32k context long model.
[08:21] Rina Gupta: since we'll be on-prem, how do GPU memory and host RAM change the knobs?
[08:27] Luca Ortiz: lower GPU memory means lower max_num_seqs and smaller batch_token_cap. On host RAM constraints, you might choose to keep KV cache on disk with LRU reservoir which increases latency for cold hits — not ideal for p99. If possible, we recommend provisioning enough host RAM to keep hot-set in memory.
[08:46] Priya Nair: what's your guidance for max_num_seqs vs GPU type?
[08:50] Luca Ortiz: for A100 80G you can push max_num_seqs to 128 for short tokens; for 40G more conservative ~64; for Ampere-based smaller cards maybe 32. But again depends on quantization and kv cache residency.
[09:06] Evan Cole: can we set dynamic knob based on observed latency? like auto-scale max_num_seqs down when p99 creeps?
[09:12] Luca Ortiz: yes we support automatic scheduler policies: a simple closed-loop controller reducing max_num_seqs or idle_ms when p99 breaches thresholds, and increasing when headroom exists. It's part of Redwood Optimize policies.
[09:25] Priya Nair: brilliant. what's the timeframe to implement an auto policy in our Dedicated cluster?
[09:30] Maya Chen: config-level it's minutes; we can propose a conservative policy and test in staging in a week.
[09:36] Evan Cole: earlier you mentioned queue high-water in token-equivalents — how do you map request size to tokens if some of our traffic is non-English or has emojis?
[09:45] Luca Ortiz: tokenizer mapping is deterministic; we sample your trace for token distribution. emojis tend to tokenize into 1-2 tokens typically. For non-English it's model/tokenizer dependent but we include that in the trace profiling step.
[09:59] Rina Gupta: any caveats for Kubernetes + on-prem deployments? e.g., pod eviction causing kv cache loss creating cold misses?
[10:05] Luca Ortiz: yes pod eviction is painful — for on-prem we recommend StatefulSets with local PV for cache shards, and affinity rules to avoid scheduling on preemptible hosts. Also configure graceful shutdown hooks to flush hot keys if needed.
[10:19] Priya Nair: good. can we set the scheduler to prefer local-execution to minimize cross-host network?
[10:23] Luca Ortiz: yes — scheduling locality policies allow biasing compute to hosts that already hold the kv shard; that reduces network fetches.
[10:29] Maya Chen: interrupting — practical next steps: Luca will run a throughput sweep and Maya will share security docs.
[10:36] Priya Nair: sounds good. Evan, Rina — any final technical asks?
[10:40] Evan Cole: would like the CSV with batch_token_cap permutations and p50/p95/p99.
[10:45] Rina Gupta: and an example k8s StatefulSet manifest for pinned cache.
[10:49] Luca Ortiz: will do both. we'll also include example config for auto-scaler policy to tweak max_num_seqs on the fly.
[10:57] Priya Nair: one more thing — how do you instrument cache hit rate for a specific user/session?
[11:02] Luca Ortiz: we export per-session cache hit metrics and you can tag requests with session_id; Console shows hit rate histograms and cold miss traces.
[11:11] Maya Chen: okay, wrapping — recap of agreed actions and follow-ups:
[11:16] Priya Nair: thank you, appreciate it.
